title: Believing what you’re told: politeness and scalar inferences

source.title: Believing what you’re told: politeness and scalar inferences

studies.title: Study 1 · Speech and interpretation
studies.description: Compare context and two kinds of interpretation questions.

studies.title: Study 2 · Clarified context
studies.description: Clarify the speaker’s knowledge and retain the compatibility question.

fields.label: Why this research?
fields.value: When someone says “some”, does politeness change what a listener understands, or whether the listener believes it? Earlier work treated answers to a compatibility question as evidence of comprehension. This paper separates comprehension from acceptance of a speaker’s message.

fields.label: What did the authors predict?
fields.value: Face-threatening messages can trigger a “not all” inference that listeners subsequently reject as untrustworthy. The authors predict additional time at the later question/epistemic-assessment stage, rather than the utterance/comprehension stage. The two studies also examine categorical responses and the effect of clarifying the story.

fields.label: How the studies connect
fields.value: Both studies compare face-threat and face-boost versions between participants. Study 1 separates the story, utterance and questions and includes a conversational-implicature question. Study 2 clarifies the speaker’s knowledge and the listener’s purpose, and removes that extra question. The studies are related tests, not two experimental conditions.

fields.label: Who took part?
fields.value: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers: Study 1 recruited 399 and analysed 292 participants; Study 2 recruited 398 and analysed 294. The paper reports exclusions involving reading/response behaviour. Recruited and analysed counts are kept separate in the experiment protocol.

fields.label: What participants encountered
fields.value: A speech vignette and Denise’s comment that some people hated or loved the speech. Study-specific wording and questions are printed in the paper and Appendix A. The participant preview uses those original texts; this research summary is not shown to simulated participants.

fields.label: What happened?
fields.value: Participants read the vignette, then the utterance, then answer the semantic-compatibility question. Study 1 adds a question about giving the speech again. The original study collected separate reaction times. Exact executable screens and ordering belong to the linked protocol.

fields.label: What was measured?
fields.value: The manipulated context is face-threat versus face-boost. Outcomes include Yes/No compatibility responses, the Study 1 conversational-implicature response and original reaction-time measures. Compatibility responses alone must not be equated with direct observation of comprehension.

fields.label: What can we compare?
fields.value: The current environment supports categorical response proportions and the declared within-study contrasts. The original paper also reports reaction-time analyses and logistic regressions; those are outside this environment’s supported replay. Timing/click exclusions cannot be claimed reproduced by this text-only replay.
fields.derivation: Supported replay scope is read from protocol.analysis and protocol.omitted; it is distinct from the paper’s complete analysis.

fields.label: What did the paper report?
fields.value: Study 1: compatibility Yes responses were 45% for face-threat and 32% for face-boost; the speech-again question yielded 7% versus 64% Yes. Study 2: compatibility Yes responses were 45% versus 12.5%. These are reported human results, not new simulation outputs; exact computable targets and contrasts are referenced from the protocol.

fields.label: What is the main takeaway?
fields.value: The authors argue that understanding an implied message and accepting it as true are distinct processes. They locate the face-threat slowdown in epistemic assessment rather than comprehension. A categorical-only AI trial would test only part of that account; matching its response percentages would not establish the proposed mechanism.
fields.derivation: The final sentence limits what our categorical replay can establish; it does not claim the paper tested AI participants.

fields.label: What remains open?
fields.value: The paper calls for paradigms that more clearly separate comprehension and epistemic assessment. Our replay additionally omits reaction-time analyses and unavailable consent/control/debrief wording. Those replay omissions are not presented as limitations stated by the authors, and the current scholarly pilot is not independently reviewed.
fields.derivation: Distinguishes the authors’ future-work statement from the declared implementation scope and review status.

evidence.quote: In two experiments, we test the hypothesis that, in these face-threatening contexts, scalar inferences are largely derived but are less likely to be accepted as true.

Study 1 relies on Bonnefon et al.’s (2011) original materials, while Study 2 introduces some motivated changes to the materials in order to increase the likelihood that the scalar inference would be effectively derived.
We recruited 399 participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk
In the face-boost condition, participants were more divided: 36% said “No” and 64% answered “Yes.”
There was no conversational implicature question.
The challenge for the future is to devise new paradigms to study comprehension and epistemic assessment as two distinct components in the process of forming beliefs via testimony.

scholarly.review: Curated pilot; scholarly source fidelity has not received independent review.
